title: Meet the Mediators
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos introduces 'mediators' -- educators who can contextualize the contentious science-of-reading debates without retreating into either camp's polemics -- using herself and David Reinking as primary examples. The article opens with a personal narrative: twenty years ago, Janetos taught her neighbor's grandson to read in sixteen hours using the Phono-Graphix (LP) approach, demonstrating that a principled but simplified phonics method produces dramatic results without requiring instruction in all of English orthography. The core of the article is an extended engagement with the Reinkings' new compendium of English sound-symbol correspondences, which catalogs the full complexity of English phonics not to argue against teaching it but to demonstrate that not all of it can or should be explicitly taught. Janetos excerpts the compendium's major concessions: teachers must decide which phonics to prioritize, when to stop explicit instruction, and how to help students reach 'escape velocity' -- the point where self-teaching through reading replaces formal phonics instruction. The piece argues that mediators are valuable precisely because they can say both 'teach phonics' and 'don't over-teach it' while explaining coherently why both are simultaneously true -- and that the Reinkings' compendium is at least as useful as a guide for what NOT to teach as for what to teach.
points: * Janetos defines 'mediators' as educators who can hold genuine complexity about reading instruction -- acknowledging that phonics is essential AND that over-teaching phonics has real costs -- without being captured by either side's polemics. * Her personal Phono-Graphix intervention demonstrates the core mediator principle: sixteen hours of principled, well-sequenced phonics with application always in text produced a complete reading turnaround -- without exhaustive coverage of all English orthography, because reading practice teaches patterns that explicit lessons don't. * The Reinkings' compendium explicitly states it is 'at least as useful' as a guide for what NOT to teach as for what to teach: English phonics complexity is so vast that attempting full explicit coverage would exhaust instructional time without serving developing readers. * The concept of 'escape velocity' -- the reader's transition from formal phonics instruction to automatic, self-teaching decoding -- explains why explicit phonics has a productive endpoint: once the reader can learn patterns independently through reading, continued explicit instruction becomes opportunity cost. * The key practical questions the compendium surfaces but cannot fully answer -- when to start phonics, when to stop, which patterns to prioritize -- remain empirically open, which is exactly why teacher knowledge and professional judgment remain irreplaceable even within a structured phonics framework.
quotes: I had my teacher's guide, my PG kit -- and my paint strips. Compared to the tomes from a popular ELA program that I had been given while teaching first grade, my spiral-bound PG manual looked like an instructional guide on GLP-1s -- but it still contained all the (pared down) essentials of teaching a child how to encode and decode.

Lucky for both of us, by the end of summer my pupil -- my pal -- was reading and flew through first grade on grade level and never looked back. Children learn what they are taught, Diane McGuinness writes in Early Reading Instruction: What Science Really Tells Us About How to Teach Reading -- so I taught him to read words instead of pictures.

Our purpose in constructing the compendium was not just to validate and illustrate our point that those complex correspondences present inordinate challenges to teaching, learning, and applying phonics. In the spirit of our previous article, we were also motivated by the belief that the compendium could be a useful resource for teachers and others involved in teaching phonics when deciding what, how, and how much phonics to teach.

Another point we made in our previous article: It is not reasonable to teach all phonics in English along with its many idiosyncrasies and exceptions. Even the most zealous advocate of teaching phonics would not advocate teaching explicitly the full complexity of Tables 1 and 2 here. Thus, emphatically, we do not intend the compendium to become a guide for what phonics to teach.

In fact, the compendium may be at least as useful in doing the opposite. It is as much a guide for what phonics is likely to be too confusing and difficult to teach as much as it is to suggest what to teach. In that vein, teaching elementary phonics in English is, as some have put it, an 'on-ramp' to reading that allows developing readers to gradually shift to using a larger repertoire of sophisticated skills to enable automatic decoding and fluency.

Of necessity, new readers in English must figure out many of the nuances of phonics on their own. Further, becoming a fluent reader means gradually putting aside almost entirely any conscious use of phonics. Seidenberg has described moving from formal instruction to informal independent acquisition of all phonics as achieving 'escape velocity,' like a rocket leaving earth's gravitational pull and requiring no more thrust from its engines.

There is virtually no research addressing such questions directly, in part, we contend, because there is not a full understanding, nor appreciation of, the complexity of English in connecting sounds and letters. We do not claim that our compendium provides perfectly clear and explicit answers. But, it does convincingly bring them to the forefront of consideration and may be a useful resource in making informed decisions about which letter-sound relations might fit better.

If we're trying to decide whether to teach something, there's the main question: How often does it occur? How many words does it apply to? What you have to do at a certain point is decide, what's the return on investment...The sweet spot was somewhere between about 95 and 110 sound-spelling patterns.
